summary:
Consensual same-sex sexual acts between adults in private are legal in Côte d'Ivoire and have never been criminalised. The country's historic-era legal inheritance did not include sodomy offences, and no statute criminalising private same-sex conduct has been enacted since.

Article 360 of the Penal Code punishes a public breach of decency with three months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 500,000 francs. Where the breach consists of an indecent or act contrary to nature with an individual of the same sex, the penalty rises to six months to two years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 to 300,000 francs, doubled where the act is committed against a minor or in the presence of a minor under eighteen. Under Articles 358 and 359 the age of consent is 18 for same-sex couples and 15 for different-sex couples, so conduct involving a same-sex partner aged between 15 and 17 is an offence regardless of consent.

Côte d'Ivoire provides no legal protection against discrimination on the basis of gender identity, and none on the basis of sexual orientation. The government does not recognise same-sex couples, and gay and lesbian individuals and couples are not legally recognised as eligible to adopt.

Official posture is mixed. In March 2010 the Ivorian representative stated that the country would begin taking measures to ensure non-discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, while ruling out awareness-raising programmes as not a current priority. In September 2024 the National Human Rights Council called on the public to refrain from online hatred and violence toward woubi (gay men and trans women) and lelé (lesbians and trans men), stating that despite their sexual orientation the members of that community remain human beings entitled to the rights enshrined in the Constitution and in international human rights treaties. Against this, in 2024 President Alassane Ouattara promised to introduce a bill to Parliament to counter the expansion of homosexuality.

Violence concentrates on gender expression rather than on sexual orientation alone. Transgender women and other feminine-presenting people assigned male at birth face especially hostile attention because their presentation breaches social norms, and travestis have been documented as facing harsher stigmatisation and violence than sexual minorities whose gender conformity keeps them unremarked. During the 2010-2011 post-electoral crisis the Force Républicaines de Côte d'Ivoire beat and abused gay men and transgender persons, most of them sex workers; complaints were not filed for fear of reprisals, and fighters were more aggressive toward transvestis. In 2012 FRCI members repeatedly raided Le Club, a bar frequented by gender and sexual minorities and mainly targeting effeminate men and transvestis, forcing them into a cargo truck, sometimes compelling them to remove clothing and demanding a substantial fine under threat of being taken to base.

A documented surge of violence occurred in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024, when 45 assault incidents were recorded in the city. Social media influencers called for violence, a hoax circulated that the French President had asked the Ivorian President to legalise same-sex marriage, and a homophobia-motivated attack struck a market employing gay hair stylists. Afterward people avoided going out during the day and meeting in public and remained hypervigilant. The figure of 45 incidents is a raw count for one city over roughly seven weeks; the sources give no population denominator and no comparison with the general assault or homicide rate, so it indicates a documented cluster rather than a measurable per-capita risk.

Police and state responses are a recurring barrier. The US State Department's 2023 report found that same-sex conduct is not criminalised but that LGBTQI+ persons faced violence, including three deaths reported within the community during the year; police responses to non-state violence were sometimes slow and ineffective and often blamed the victim. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, Abidjan, while walking with another man. Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years, but as of 2023 many people still did not report to police, believing they would not be taken seriously.

Reported conversion therapy in 2023 included a transgender man attempting suicide after being forced to attend a prayer camp. Many transgender people lack secure housing.

Discrimination continues in healthcare, housing and employment. Documented consequences include evictions and family expulsions causing school dropout, refusal to hire or promote, and dismissal if a person is discovered; a doctor refused service on grounds of sexual orientation until protest led to care being provided. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preach against the community.
tangentialFactors:
The social climate is described as hostile to sexual and gender minorities on the grounds that their identities are seen as abnormal and as originating in the Global North. Wealthier people are treated with less hostility than poorer ones, which shapes how exposure to risk is distributed. A vocal minority of Muslim and Christian leaders preaches against the community.

Reporting on the country has intensified alongside the documented 2024 violence: a New York Times article of October 2024 addressed the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire, and a UNDP report of December 2024, African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa, includes a Côte d'Ivoire country overview assessing the protective legal environment, investigation and prosecution of perpetrators, access to justice, civic space and inclusion.

The US State Department's 2011 human rights report for Côte d'Ivoire contains limited LGBT-specific content and instead covers the post-electoral crisis context, including some 3,000 deaths, sexual violence and displacement. That crisis is the backdrop against which the documented abuse of gay and transgender people by the Force Républicaines de Côte d'Ivoire occurred.

The only quoted assessment of societal tolerance concerns gay people rather than transgender people: one source records that there is still discrimination against gay people but that the country is generally moving toward relative tolerance. No equivalent assessment for transgender people appears in the inventory.
localsOnly:
Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation, and no legal recognition of same-sex couples or of their eligibility to adopt. The unequal age of consent under Articles 358 and 359, 18 for same-sex and 15 for different-sex couples, applies to residents as well as visitors.

Travestis and other gender non-conforming people assigned male at birth have historically been underserved by Ivorian rights groups, which distanced themselves from them, and they experience isolation documented alongside the 2010-11 post-election violence. Their stigmatisation is harsher than that faced by sexual minorities whose gender conformity avoids attention.

Reporting violence to police is uncommon. Complaints from the 2010-2011 period were not filed for fear of reprisals, and as of 2023 many residents still did not approach police, believing they would not be taken seriously, with accounts of officers failing to treat violence seriously and blaming victims. Authorities were described as somewhat better at handling complaints than in previous years.

Residents face discrimination across healthcare, housing, employment and schooling, with evictions and family expulsions leading to school dropout, and refusal to hire, refusal to promote or dismissal where a person is discovered. Housing insecurity is widespread among transgender people, and conversion therapy has been reported, including a 2023 case in which a transgender man attempted suicide after being forced to attend a prayer camp.

The National Human Rights Council's September 2024 statement is the principal recent institutional expression of protection, addressing online hatred and violence toward woubi and lelé communities. The 2024 presidential commitment to a bill countering the expansion of homosexuality points in the opposite direction, and no text or status of such a bill is given in the sources.
outOfScopeNotes:
Placement of transgender detainees is unresolved. Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire; where trans detainees are placed, whether by birth sex or identity, whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any available publication. On the Human Rights Watch country page for Côte d'Ivoire, LGBT Rights appears only as a topic-facet link.

No source in the inventory addresses legal gender recognition, amendment of gender markers on national identity documents or passports, or entry, visa and border-screening treatment of transgender travellers. Any assessment of those questions would be unsourced.

The violence counts available are raw counts without denominators. The 45 assault incidents recorded in Abidjan between early September and late October 2024 and the three deaths reported within the LGBTQI+ community in 2023 are not accompanied by population figures, general homicide or assault rates, or undercount estimates, so neither can be converted into a comparative risk magnitude.

No source documents societal tolerance toward transgender people specifically. The only tolerance assessment quoted concerns gay people, and the inventory contains no equivalent statement, survey or finding for trans residents or visitors.

The 2024 promise of a bill to counter the expansion of homosexuality is recorded without a bill text, parliamentary status, or date, so its content and current standing remain unresolved.
